lessons.title: Welcome to BE106!
lessons.refined:
IN PLAIN WORDS
BE106 is the backend capstone: build one complete API by yourself, run it at a live public URL, keep it in a public GitHub repository with docs a stranger can follow, and be able to explain every line, even code AI helped with.

KEY IDEAS
1. From guided practice to shipping one complete backend on your own.
2. Deliverables: a live URL for the running API and a public GitHub repository.
3. Documentation good enough for another developer to use the API.
4. AI is allowed, but you must be able to explain every line you keep.

KEY POINTS
- One API, running publicly, in a public repository, documented.
- Idea → end-to-end backend → hosted → documented → explained.

lessons.title: Scoping your project idea
lessons.refined:
IN PLAIN WORDS
Scope a project small enough for one term: one user type and one core resource. Your idea was Boost: each user saves short motivational messages ("boosts") and taps a button to see one. Each boost belongs to the user who made it.

KEY IDEAS
1. Resource domain: the real-world area the app is about (motivation and self-esteem).
2. Core resource: the main thing the backend stores (a boost, a short message).
3. Record ownership: which user owns each record (the one who created the boost).
4. User story: who uses it, what they do, and why.
5. Term-sized scope: one user type, one resource, basic actions, no extra services or real-time features.

CODE
```text
Domain:     motivation / self-esteem
Resource:   boost = a short motivational message
Owner:      the user who created it
Actions:    create, view, edit, delete, show one on a button tap
User story: As a user who wants to stay motivated, I want to save my own boosts
            and tap a button to see one, so I get a quick reminder when I'm feeling low.
```

KEY POINTS
- Start with a tight core loop, then build on it.
- One user type + one resource + basic actions fits one term.

NOTE
Later lessons build Studio Cost Raid (studio_cost_raid) instead of Boost. If you switched projects, this plan describes the first idea.

lessons.title: API resource and endpoint planning
lessons.refined:
IN PLAIN WORDS
Plan the API before coding it: which method does what, which status code means success, and which means each kind of error. Auth endpoints: register, login, profile. Resource endpoints: list, create, get one, update, delete, plus a random "lucky" one.

KEY IDEAS
1. GET reads, POST creates, PUT updates, DELETE removes.
2. 200 OK returns data. 201 Created made something. 204 No Content succeeded with nothing to return.
3. 400 bad input. 401 not logged in or bad token. 403 logged in but not allowed. 404 doesn't exist, or isn't visible to you.

CODE
```text
Auth
POST /api/register     create an account      201 | 400, 409 email taken   public
POST /api/login        check credentials      200 | 400, 401               public
GET  /api/profile      current user           200 | 401                    logged in

Boosts (all logged in)
GET    /api/boosts               list mine              200 | 401
POST   /api/boosts               create                 201 | 400, 401
GET    /api/boosts/<id>          one boost              200 | 401, 404
PUT    /api/boosts/<id>          update                 200 | 400, 401, 404
DELETE /api/boosts/<id>          delete                 204 | 401, 404
GET    /api/boosts/luckyboost    one random boost       200 | 401, 404 (none yet)
```

KEY POINTS
- 401 = who are you? 403 = you can't do this.
- Profile → 200. Create → 201. Delete → 204.

lessons.title: Virtual environment and dependencies
lessons.refined:
IN PLAIN WORDS
A virtual environment is a private Python setup for one project. Create it, activate it, and prove it's active with sys.executable. Install packages, then pin exact versions with pip freeze > requirements.txt, so anyone can rebuild the same environment.

KEY IDEAS
1. A venv keeps each project's packages separate.
2. The (venv) prompt is a hint; the real proof is sys.executable pointing inside the project's venv.
3. A venv is tied to the Python version that created it.
4. Pinned = package==exact_version on every line.
5. requirements.txt stores the package list, not the venv. You still create and activate a venv before installing from it.

STEPS
1. python -m venv venv
2. Activate it (PowerShell: .\venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1).
3. python -c "import sys; print(sys.executable)" → the path should be inside your project's venv.
4. Install the packages.
5. pip freeze > requirements.txt
6. Elsewhere: new venv, activate, pip install -r requirements.txt.

CODE
```powershell
python -m venv venv
.\venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1
python -c "import sys; print(sys.executable)"
pip install flask flask-sqlalchemy flask-migrate python-dotenv pyjwt
pip freeze > requirements.txt
```

KEY POINTS
- Same pinned versions everywhere means fewer "works on my machine" bugs.

lessons.title: Application factory skeleton
lessons.refined:
IN PLAIN WORDS
The project skeleton: extensions.py creates db and migrate without an app, __init__.py has create_app (build the app, set the database, init the extensions, register the blueprint), and main.py defines the blueprint. Check it with flask routes.

KEY IDEAS
1. Extensions are created once and bound to each app inside the factory.
2. A factory lets dev, test and production apps come from the same code.

CODE
```text
studio_cost_raid/
  __init__.py       # app factory
  extensions.py     # db and migrate objects
  main.py           # blueprint
```

```python
# extensions.py
from flask_sqlalchemy import SQLAlchemy
from flask_migrate import Migrate
db = SQLAlchemy()
migrate = Migrate()

# main.py
from flask import Blueprint
main_bp = Blueprint("main", __name__)

# __init__.py
from flask import Flask
from .extensions import db, migrate
from .main import main_bp

def create_app(config_name="development"):
    app = Flask(__name__)
    app.config["SQLALCHEMY_DATABASE_URI"] = "sqlite:///dev.db"
    db.init_app(app)
    migrate.init_app(app, db)
    app.register_blueprint(main_bp)
    return app
```

```powershell
.\venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1
$env:FLASK_APP = "studio_cost_raid:create_app"
flask routes
```

KEY POINTS
- create_app builds and returns a ready app; nothing is built at import time.

lessons.title: Config classes and .env
lessons.refined:
IN PLAIN WORDS
Three config classes (Development, Testing, Production) read values with os.getenv, with safe fallbacks for dev and test only. config_map picks a class by name, and from_object copies its UPPERCASE attributes. .env holds your real local values; .env.example holds the same keys with placeholders. Load .env before the config classes are imported.

KEY IDEAS
1. Three classes for three environments; UPPERCASE attributes become Flask config keys.
2. Dev and test may have harmless fallbacks. Production reads only real environment variables.
3. config_name → config_map[config_name] → app.config.from_object(cls).
4. .env: real values, local only, never committed. .env.example: same keys, placeholder values, committed.
5. Use os.getenv in config classes. os.environ["X"] crashes at import if X is missing.
6. Moving to Postgres later only means changing DATABASE_URL.

CODE
```python
# config.py (project root)
import os

class DevelopmentConfig:
    DEBUG = True
    SQLALCHEMY_DATABASE_URI = os.getenv("DATABASE_URL", "sqlite:///dev.db")
    JWT_SECRET_KEY = os.getenv("JWT_SECRET_KEY", "dev-secret-not-for-prod")

class TestingConfig:
    TESTING = True
    SQLALCHEMY_DATABASE_URI = os.getenv("TEST_DATABASE_URL", "sqlite:///test.db")
    JWT_SECRET_KEY = os.getenv("JWT_SECRET_KEY", "test-secret-not-for-prod")

class ProductionConfig:
    SQLALCHEMY_DATABASE_URI = os.getenv("DATABASE_URL")
    JWT_SECRET_KEY = os.getenv("JWT_SECRET_KEY")

config_map = {"development": DevelopmentConfig, "testing": TestingConfig, "production": ProductionConfig}
```

```python
# studio_cost_raid/__init__.py
from dotenv import load_dotenv
load_dotenv()                          # FIRST: before config.py is imported

from flask import Flask
from config import config_map
from .extensions import db, migrate
from .main import main_bp

def create_app(config_name="development"):
    app = Flask(__name__)
    app.config.from_object(config_map[config_name])
    db.init_app(app)
    migrate.init_app(app, db)
    app.register_blueprint(main_bp)
    return app
```

```text
# .env.example (committed)
DATABASE_URL=sqlite:///dev.db
JWT_SECRET_KEY=your-jwt-secret-here
FLASK_DEBUG=1
```

KEY POINTS
- ModuleNotFoundError: 'config' → config.py must sit in the project root, next to run.py.
- Later: DATABASE_URL=postgresql+psycopg2://user:password@host:port/dbname, no Python changes.

CORRECTION
- The lesson's code imported config before calling load_dotenv(). Class attributes are read once, at import, so they never saw your .env values and fell back to the defaults. Checked by running it: imported first → sqlite:///dev.db; load_dotenv first → sqlite:///dev2.db. It only seemed to work because the flask command loads .env by itself when python-dotenv is installed. python run.py doesn't.
- FLASK_ENV was removed in Flask 2.3. FLASK_DEBUG=1 turns on debug mode.

lessons.title: Git init and .gitignore
lessons.refined:
IN PLAIN WORDS
git init, then write .gitignore (venv/, .env, __pycache__/, instance/*.db) before the first commit, and check with git status that ignored files don't show. Commit, then check git log --oneline.

KEY IDEAS
1. Ignored file: exists on disk; Git acts as if it doesn't.
2. Tracked file: added at least once; its changes show in git status.
3. Commit: a snapshot in history. Push: uploads existing commits; it doesn't create them.
4. Changing .gitignore doesn't remove anything already committed. Ignore .env before its first commit.

STEPS
1. git init
2. Write .gitignore.
3. git status: .env and venv/ must not appear.
4. git add . and git commit -m "Initial project structure with config and Flask skeleton"
5. git log --oneline

CODE
```gitignore
venv/
.env
__pycache__/
instance/*.db
```

KEY POINTS
- Ignore secrets before the first commit, not after.

lessons.title: Branching and commit hygiene
lessons.refined:
IN PLAIN WORDS
Keep main always runnable. Do each piece of work on its own branch, write focused commits that say why, and merge with --no-ff so the branch shows in the history. Delete the branch locally and on GitHub after merging.

STEPS
1. git switch -c branch-name (new branch from where you are).
2. Make focused commits.
3. git push -u origin branch-name (push and link local ↔ remote).
4. On main: git merge --no-ff branch-name -m "Merge branch-name: short reason"
5. git push, then git log --oneline --graph to see the merge.
6. git branch -d branch-name and git push origin --delete branch-name.

CODE
```bash
git switch -c docs-readme
git commit -m "Document local dev setup in README"
git push -u origin docs-readme
git branch -vv                     # branches, last commit, what each tracks
git switch main
git merge --no-ff docs-readme -m "Merge docs-readme: setup docs"
git push
git log --oneline --graph
git branch -d docs-readme
git push origin --delete docs-readme
```

KEY POINTS
- Commit message pattern: verb + what + why. If a stranger can't tell why the change exists, the message is too weak.
- --no-ff forces a merge commit, so the branch stays visible in the graph.

lessons.title: Project file tree and README
lessons.refined:
IN PLAIN WORDS
The finished setup: the app package, instance/, config.py, requirements.txt, run.py, .env (local only), .env.example, .gitignore, and a README a stranger can follow to clone and run the project. Audit what Git tracks and what it ignores.

KEY IDEAS
1. venv/, __pycache__/, .env and instance/*.db exist locally but are ignored.
2. .env.example lists every variable with a placeholder.
3. README: clone-and-run steps, each environment variable, and the migration commands.

STEPS
1. git ls-files: what's tracked.
2. git status --ignored --short: what's ignored.
3. Secrets and local files should be on disk but not in Git.

CODE
```gitignore
venv/
.env
__pycache__/
**/__pycache__/
instance/*.db
```

```powershell
# README: clone and run
git clone <REPO_URL>
cd studio-cost-raid-backend
python -m venv venv
.\venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1
pip install -r requirements.txt
copy .env.example .env          # then fill in real values
flask db upgrade
python run.py
```

KEY POINTS
- A stranger should be able to run the project from the README alone.
- Never commit real secrets.

lessons.title: First health-check endpoint
lessons.refined:
IN PLAIN WORDS
GET /health returns {"status": "ok"} with 200. The request goes: client → app from create_app → blueprint → health() → JSON. Code isn't done until a real request returns the expected result, and only then do you commit.

CODE
```python
# main.py
from flask import Blueprint, jsonify

main_bp = Blueprint("main", __name__)

@main_bp.get("/health")
def health():
    return jsonify({"status": "ok"}), 200
```

```powershell
python run.py
curl.exe http://127.0.0.1:5000/health        # {"status": "ok"}
git add studio_cost_raid/main.py
git commit -m "Add /health endpoint for service health-check"
```

KEY POINTS
- A real response is stronger evidence than code that looks right.
- In PowerShell, use curl.exe; plain curl is a different command there.

lessons.title: Challenge: skeleton smoke test
lessons.refined:
IN PLAIN WORDS
Smoke test the skeleton: the server starts, a startup message shows which config loaded, /health answers through real HTTP, and git status and git log show a clean tree and a clear history.

STEPS
1. python run.py → "Running on http://127.0.0.1:5000" proves the factory and Flask start.
2. Print the loaded config name at startup to prove the right environment.
3. curl.exe http://127.0.0.1:5000/health → {"status": "ok"} proves the route works.
4. git status → "nothing to commit, working tree clean".
5. git log --oneline --decorate --graph -n 5 → a short, readable history.

KEY POINTS
- Each check proves one layer: startup, config, route, history.

lessons.title: User model and migration
lessons.refined:
IN PLAIN WORDS
User model: id, email (unique, required), password_hash (required), created_at. Run the migration chain (init → migrate → upgrade), then check the real database: db.engine.url shows which file is in use, and PRAGMA table_info(user) should match the model.

KEY IDEAS
1. The models must be imported by the app (from . import models) so migrations see them.
2. When there are several database files, ask SQLAlchemy which one it uses instead of guessing.
3. PRAGMA table_info columns: name, type, notnull (1 = required), pk (1 = primary key).

STEPS
1. flask --app run.py db init (once).
2. flask --app run.py db migrate -m "Add User model"
3. flask --app run.py db upgrade
4. flask --app run.py shell → print(db.engine.url)
5. Open that file and run PRAGMA table_info(user).

CODE
```python
from .extensions import db

class User(db.Model):
    id = db.Column(db.Integer, primary_key=True)
    email = db.Column(db.String(255), unique=True, nullable=False)
    password_hash = db.Column(db.String(255), nullable=False)
    created_at = db.Column(db.DateTime)
```

```python
# inside flask shell
from studio_cost_raid.extensions import db
print(db.engine.url)            # e.g. sqlite:///...instance/dev2.db
```

```sql
SELECT name FROM sqlite_master WHERE type='table';
PRAGMA table_info(user);
```

KEY POINTS
- Verify the schema in the database the app really uses.
- python -m sqlite3 doesn't support dot-commands like .schema; use PRAGMA instead.

lessons.title: Registration endpoint and validation
Password hashing
lessons.refined:
IN PLAIN WORDS
Store only one-way Werkzeug scrypt hashes. check_password_hash(stored, guess) returns True or False, and nothing is ever decrypted. Audit the database: every password_hash should start with "scrypt:".

STEPS: LOGIN CHECK
1. Find the user by email.
2. Not found → login fails.
3. check_password_hash(stored_hash, entered_password).
4. True → success. False → failure.

CODE
```python
from werkzeug.security import generate_password_hash, check_password_hash

user.password_hash = generate_password_hash(plain_password)      # registration
is_valid = check_password_hash(user.password_hash, candidate)     # login: True or False
```

```python
# audit: every row should print True
for u in db.session.execute(db.select(User)).scalars():
    print(u.id, u.email, u.password_hash.startswith("scrypt:"))
```

KEY POINTS
- A hash can't be reversed; you can only test guesses against it.
- A row that prints False needs fixing (delete and re-register through the normal flow).

lessons.title: Login and JWT issuance
lessons.refined:
IN PLAIN WORDS
Login validates the input, finds the user and checks the password. An unknown email and a wrong password both get the same 401 INVALID_CREDENTIALS. On success, the token holds sub = str(user.id), role and exp (now + the lifetime from config), signed with HS256, and is returned as {"access_token": ...}.

KEY IDEAS
1. sub = who (the user id, as a string). exp = valid until.
2. The secret and lifetime come from config, not from the code.
3. Decoding without verifying is for looking inside a token while debugging, never for trusting it.

CODE
```python
import datetime as dt
import jwt
from flask import current_app

secret = current_app.config["JWT_SECRET_KEY"]
lifetime = current_app.config["JWT_ACCESS_TOKEN_LIFETIME_SECONDS"]
payload = {
    "sub": str(user.id),
    "role": user.role,
    "exp": dt.datetime.now(dt.timezone.utc) + dt.timedelta(seconds=lifetime),
}
token = jwt.encode(payload, secret, algorithm="HS256")
return jsonify({"access_token": token}), 200
```

```python
# debugging only: read a token without checking it
jwt.decode(token, options={"verify_signature": False})
# {'sub': '4', 'role': 'player', 'exp': 1795250369}
```

```json
{"error": {"code": "INVALID_CREDENTIALS", "message": "Invalid email or password"}}
```

KEY POINTS
- The same 401 for unknown email and wrong password.
- Secrets and lifetimes live in config classes, per environment.

lessons.title: Protecting routes with decorators
Token expiry and rejection
lessons.refined:
IN PLAIN WORDS
The token lifetime comes from config. An expired token raises jwt.ExpiredSignatureError → 401 TOKEN_EXPIRED, caught before the general PyJWTError → 401 INVALID_TOKEN. Expiry limits how long a stolen token works. Stateless logout can't cancel one specific token.

CODE
```python
try:
    payload = jwt.decode(token, secret, algorithms=["HS256"])
    g.user_id = int(payload["sub"])
except jwt.ExpiredSignatureError:                     # must come first
    return jsonify({"error": {"code": "TOKEN_EXPIRED", "message": "Token has expired"}}), 401
except jwt.PyJWTError:
    return jsonify({"error": {"code": "INVALID_TOKEN", "message": "Invalid token"}}), 401
```

KEY POINTS
- ExpiredSignatureError is a kind of PyJWTError; catch it first or the general one swallows it.
- A stolen but valid token works only until exp.
- With no stored sessions, the server can't switch off one issued token.
- A short lifetime (like 60 seconds) is handy for testing expiry; restore the normal one afterwards.

lessons.title: Profile read and update endpoints
Roles and admin access
lessons.refined:
IN PLAIN WORDS
Users get a role (default "user", NOT NULL). The migration adds it with server_default='user', fills old rows, then sets NOT NULL. The token check (authentication, 401) lives in @require_auth; the role check (authorization, 403) lives in the route. Make admins only through flask shell or a CLI command, never a public endpoint.

STEPS: ADD A REQUIRED COLUMN TO A TABLE WITH ROWS
1. Add the column to the model: nullable=False, default="user".
2. In the migration, add it with server_default='user'.
3. Fill any existing rows: UPDATE user SET role = 'user' WHERE role IS NULL.
4. Then make it NOT NULL.

STEPS: AN ADMIN-ONLY ROUTE
1. @require_auth (no or bad token → 401).
2. Load the user (or read the role).
3. role != "admin" → 403.
4. Otherwise → 200.

CODE
```python
role = db.Column(db.String(50), nullable=False, default="user")
```

```python
@admin_bp.get("/admin/stats")
@require_auth
def admin_stats():
    user = db.session.get(User, g.user_id)
    if user.role != "admin":
        return jsonify({"error": {"code": "FORBIDDEN", "message": "Admins only"}}), 403
    return jsonify({...}), 200
```

KEY POINTS
- SQLite refuses to add a NOT NULL column with no default ("Cannot add a NOT NULL column with default value NULL"), so use server_default.
- Never build a public "make me admin" endpoint.

lessons.title: 401 vs 403 in practice
lessons.refined:
IN PLAIN WORDS
401 means the server has no valid identity for you (missing, bad or expired token). 403 means it knows who you are, but you aren't allowed to do this. Both use the same error shape.

STEPS: PICK THE STATUS CODE
1. Is there a valid identity (a good token)? No → 401.
2. Does that identity have permission? No → 403.
3. Otherwise → 2xx.

CODE
```text
curl.exe -i http://127.0.0.1:5000/auth/users/me
HTTP/1.1 401 UNAUTHORIZED
{"error": {"code": "AUTH_REQUIRED", "message": "Authorization Bearer token required"}}
```

KEY POINTS
- Missing, bad or expired token → 401 (authentication).
- Valid token, wrong role → 403 (authorization).
- Same JSON error shape for both; only the status, code and message change.

lessons.title: Challenge: breaking your own auth
lessons.refined:
IN PLAIN WORDS
Try to break your own auth. A stolen database only holds one-way scrypt strings, not passwords. A wrong password returns 401 INVALID_CREDENTIALS, an authentication failure, because no identity was proven.

KEY IDEAS
1. Hash: one-way, used for passwords. Encryption: two-way with a key, never used to store passwords.
2. Login hashes the guess and compares; nothing is ever unscrambled.
3. Wrong password → identity not proven → 401, not 403.

STEPS
1. In flask shell, load a user and look at password_hash: only an scrypt:... string is stored.
2. With a small script, send a wrong password to the real /auth/login.
3. Expect 401 INVALID_CREDENTIALS.

CODE
```python
# flask shell
from studio_cost_raid.extensions import db
from studio_cost_raid.models import User
user = db.session.query(User).first()
print(user.password_hash)          # scrypt:32768:8:1$...
```

```python
# test_login_badpass.py
import requests
response = requests.post("http://127.0.0.1:5000/auth/login",
                         json={"email": "badpass@example.com", "password": "totally-wrong-password"})
print(response.status_code, response.json())
# 401 {'error': {'code': 'INVALID_CREDENTIALS', 'message': 'Invalid email or password'}}
```

KEY POINTS
- No plaintext password column exists.
- Unknown email and wrong password give the same 401.
- Next: more automated tests for failed auth (missing body, malformed JSON, invalid email).
